clinical_category: Traumatic brain injury rehabilitation - discharge and service coordination
blueprint_topic: Case management and continuity across inpatient, outpatient, and community rehabilitation
stem: A client with a significant traumatic brain injury will need ongoing rehabilitation and social-care services after hospital discharge. Which case-management action best supports continuity of care?

options.A: Coordinate an early multidisciplinary discharge plan, document follow-up and referrals, and identify who will be the client's key contact after discharge
options.B: Wait until the day of discharge before contacting community rehabilitation services
options.C: End coordination once the client leaves the hospital because outpatient rehabilitation should develop an unrelated plan
options.D: Limit discharge planning to insurance authorization and omit rehabilitation goals, follow-up, and community providers

rationale: A is correct. Current NICE rehabilitation guidance recommends early multidisciplinary discharge planning for people with complex rehabilitation needs after traumatic injury, reassessment of needs before discharge, coordinated and integrated support during transition to outpatient/community services, documentation of how rehabilitation will continue, and a defined point of contact or key contact after discharge when ongoing needs remain. These recommendations apply to traumatic injuries including brain injury. B delays coordination. C creates fragmentation across settings. D reduces case management to administrative authorization and omits the clinical continuity functions specified by the guideline.
educational_objective: Use case management to coordinate early multidisciplinary discharge planning, referrals, follow-up, and a clear post-discharge contact for clients with complex traumatic brain injury rehabilitation needs.
source_organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source_version_date: NICE guideline NG211 published 2022-01-18; current guidance accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NICE NG211 → Section 1.8 'Coordination of rehabilitation care at discharge': Recommendation 1.8.1 early multidisciplinary discharge planning; 1.8.2 reassess needs/review rehabilitation plan before discharge; 1.8.14 coordinated, consistent, integrated multidisciplinary approach through transfer to outpatient services; 1.8.15 document ongoing support, referrals and review appointments in rehabilitation plan/handover; 1.8.21–1.8.22 provide a single point of contact and agree a key contact when ongoing rehabilitation/health/social-care support is needed.
source_claim_supported: Current NICE guidance directly supports early multidisciplinary discharge planning, integrated transition across services, documented follow-up/referrals, and a defined post-discharge contact for people with complex traumatic-injury rehabilitation needs.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care client-needs subcategory (15–21% of items); this item tests case management, referrals, discharge planning, and continuity across care settings.
correction_summary: Total construct rebuild. The original secondary Brain Injury Association source described case management generically. The final item uses current NICE rehabilitation guidance and tests concrete coordination actions during transition from inpatient care to ongoing community rehabilitation, distinct from Q1970's immediate nurse-to-nurse handoff and Q1973's multidisciplinary needs assessment.
audit_findings: The original source was secondary and did not provide an exact current locator for the broad case-management claim.
Current NICE NG211 directly recommends early multidisciplinary discharge planning and coordinated transition to outpatient/community rehabilitation.
NICE directly supports documented follow-up/referrals and a defined post-discharge point of contact when ongoing needs remain.
The final construct is distinct from V2-Q1970 and V2-Q1973 and does not reduce case management to insurance authorization.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no unsupported outcome magnitude, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
